1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   351	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   352	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   353	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   354	
   355	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   356	
   357	```bash
   358	tail -200 /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   359	```
   360	
   361	---
   362	
   363	## Unknown extension
   364	
   365	```bash
   366	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   367	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   368	```
   369	
   370	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`
   371	says "data" and the hex doesn't match anything you recognize, ask the
   372	user what it is instead of guessing.
   373

1	# HANDOFF-18 — The Method 1.6
     2	
     3	## SELF-IDENTIFICATION (the three must agree with the files)
     4	- Written from **chat 68**, for **chat 69**. Live files: **BUILD90 main** (unchanged) and **BUILD93 compendia** (= BUILD91 + W-102 + W-103 + five instrument members; BUILD92 was an intermediate never uploaded). Register **1 to 1792**. W-103 IS seated. Chat 69 seats nothing at open; it writes W-104 for its own work at close.
     5	- Ruling (M, chat 68): instruments travel as bundle members, not as Drive tarballs. Project knowledge cannot hold this project's material; Drive stays the store, and the bundles spill to disk on download, so nothing is re-typed.
     6

324  the multiset extension of a well-founded order is well-founded. Checked against §29.2.1's own
325  movement, where six items' stake fell to nothing: the count went 13 → 10 and the multiset decreased
326  in the Dershowitz–Manna sense. **That is precisely what *the set grew and the scope descended*
327  means.**
328 
329  **P17's 1/N is derivable and the constant was dropped.** §10.3 decides whether a box lies inside Λ
330  in **seven comparisons**, against one membership test per cell for enumeration. So following the
331  bounds costs **c/N with c the number of constraints**, c = 7 here — 7/976 on Λ, 7/199,130 on Λ₁₃.
332  **And N is nowhere defined**: neither §18.4 nor Chapter 12 introduces it, so the symbol is
333  ungrounded in the sense §16.6's ⅅ_gro names. The corrected form carries no N: *following the bounds
334  costs one comparison per constraint where searching the volume costs one per cell.*
335 
336  **P22 claimed what §16.8.2 refutes.** *No lie can exist within it* is false: rebuilt around a
337  fabrication the index closes, has E = 0, is a fixed point of ℛ and satisfies every law here.
338  Restated: **in a complete index every rule is content rather than inference, so a false cell is
339  contradicted in the open by a stated rule where an inferred rule would have absorbed it. A forger's
340  remaining move is to alter a rule, and an altered rule is equally visible. A complete index
341  therefore converts deception into disagreement — error survives, concealment does not.** The index
342  cannot be lied **to**; it can be **replaced**, and replacement is an act performed on it rather than
343  a question put to it. Registers 417–420.
344 
345  Procedural — seven
346 
347 | | principle |
348 |---|---|
349 | **P4** | always audit results |
350 | **P5** | always compute the result before assuming the result |
351 | **P6** | when a question is confusing, reframe the question |
352 | **P11** | close all gaps before continuing |
353 | **P14** | a structural problem suggests a structural solution |
354 | **P15** | for fetching: use the index to navigate; data can be retrieved in pieces |
355 | **P16** | treat bounds, constraints and limits as coordinate values |
356 
357  **These have no expressions, and saying so is better than manufacturing one.** They govern how an agent uses an index, not what an index is. P15 is the exception in one respect: it has a *measure* — retrieval redundancy ρ, Chapter 19 — without being reducible to it.
358 
359  The reflexive principle
360 
361         principle                                                                                              expression
362   P1    if the index is complete, a work that comprehends it completely is itself an index, and is itself      Chapter 32
363   8     self-referencing and self-defending
364   P1    an index is complete only when there are no more questions left to answer about its                    COMPLETE(X)
365   9     contents                                                                                               ⟺ Q(X) = ∅
366   P2    the language in which a question is posed bounds whether it can close, and at what                     —
367   0     cost
368   P2    any definition contained within the lattice, and thus its equations, must be TRUE in                   —
369   1     every mathematical language and in their combinations
370   P2    because everything is defined in a complete index, the entirety of the index is                        —
371   2     visible, and no lie can exist within it
372 
373  P19, and why it is neither P7 nor P13
374  Three principles govern questions, and they are one principle in three moods. P19 was the
375  missing one.
376 
377 | | says | mood |
378 |---|---|---|
379 | **P7** | ∃N : Ω_N = ∅ | questions **can** close — possibility |
380 | **P13** | COHERENT ⟺ Ω = ∅ | coherence **may not** be claimed otherwise — prohibition |
381 | **P19** | COMPLETE ⟺ Q = ∅ | what their emptiness **buys** — definition |
382 
383  **And P19 is strictly stronger than closure.**
384 
385       E(X) = 0 says no cell the structure admits is absent. Q(X) = ∅ says no question the
386       contents admit is unanswered.
387 
388  **Λ has had E = 0 since Chapter 7 and has never had Q = ∅.** Whether *V* depends on the order of the bracket, what the Aitken bias generalises to, whether a higher-order bracket exists — **each was admitted by contents already present, and none was asked until late.**
389 
390       Closure is about what an index holds. Completeness is about what it has been asked.
391 
392  **And the condition is reachable, for the reason P7's is.** P7 was corrected once: closure requires a well-founded measure rather than a shrinking count. **Q has grown at nearly every step of this work while its scope has fallen** — from *is V novel?* to *is there an optimal order?* **The set grew and the scope descended**, and that descent is what makes P19 a criterion rather than an impossibility.
393 
394  **Q(X) = ∅ is reached not when nobody asks, but when every question the contents admit has an answer in the contents.**
395 
396  P20 — the language bounds the question
397  Three closure mechanisms are used in this book, each in a different language, each with a
398  different guarantee.
399 
400 | language | mechanism | closure | cost |

513  register records what was added and withdrawn. Enumeration is finite work and this book does it.

516  question can ever be had. A single question refutes it and nothing confirms it.

519     held until a question arrives.

input.command:
cd /home/claude/members && timeout 280 python3 - <<'EOF'
import importlib.util, math, itertools
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('tower','tower-2.py'); tw=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(tw)
L=tw.L8(); S=set(L); n=len(L)
print('|L8|',n,' C(976,2)=',n*(n-1)//2)
sums=[sum(c) for c in L]
print('coord-sum: min',min(sums),'max',max(sums),'mean %.4f'%(sum(sums)/n))
# graded rank from the bottom via covers (longest chain from the unique minimum)
bot=min(L,key=sum); print('bottom',bot, 'top candidates', [c for c in L if sum(c)==max(sums)][:3])
# covers: y covers x if y>=x coordinatewise, y!=x, and no z in S strictly between
Ls=sorted(L,key=sum)
idx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(Ls)}
import collections
rank={bot:0}
# since all constraints are monotone two-variable bounds, check whether every cover differs in exactly one coordinate by 1
def up1(c):
    for i in range(8):
        d=list(c); d[i]+=1; d=tuple(d)
        if d in S: yield d
# longest path over the unit-step graph = grading if the lattice is graded by unit steps
order=Ls
for c in order:
    if c not in rank: rank[c]=None
for c in order:
    if rank[c] is None: continue
    for d in up1(c):
        r=rank[c]+1
        if rank[d] is None or r>rank[d]: rank[d]=r
unreached=[c for c in L if rank[c] is None]
print('unit-step-unreached cells:',len(unreached), unreached[:3])
rk=[rank[c] for c in L if rank[c] is not None]
print('unit-step rank: max',max(rk),'mean %.4f'%(sum(rk)/len(rk)))
print('sum-3 mean %.4f'%(sum(sums)/n-3), ' max sum-3', max(sums)-3)
# minimal elements and maximal elements
def leq(a,b): return all(x<=y for x,y in zip(a,b))

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"568 ## 2. The protocols
569 ### 2.1 Channel construction
570 A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.
572 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.
574 ### 2.2 Admissibility
575 r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5
577 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.
579 ### 2.3 Cost resolvability
580 ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}
582 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.
584 ### 2.4 Dilution
585 cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
586 configuration
588 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.
590 ### 2.5 Census before search
591 Compute which species could work before looking for data.
593 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**
595 ### 2.6 Declines are recorded
596 A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.
598 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §23.11 gives a worked case of each.
600 ### 2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible
602 Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
603 never certifies ρ = 0.
605 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.
607 ### 2.8 Two independent routes
608 For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
609 first.
611 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 16, and it is realised
612 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §16.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
613 with no shared step.
615 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.
617 ### 2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
618 No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.
620 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.
622 ### 2.10 Retrieval
623 Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
624 cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
625 along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
626 targets are drawn from grows.
628 Chapter 19. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.
630 The second clause was added late. §30.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
631 §30.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §31.1, §31.2 and §31.3 — each made once, against
632 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.
634 Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
635 is a defect the moment it is taken.
637 ### 2.11 Provenance

# r2-ch2.py — Phase R2, main Chapter 2 (chat 69). Re-measures Chapter 2's tower-measurable figures on the
# rebuilt tower (tower-2.py beside it). Every printed line is MEASURED; the read decides.
import importlib.util, itertools, numpy as np
spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('tower','tower-2.py'); tw=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(tw)
L8=tw.L8(); S8=set(L8); L9=tw.L9(); S9=set(L9); L13=tw.L13()
def E0(X):
    A=np.array(sorted(X),dtype=np.int16); Xs=set(map(tuple,A.tolist()))
    J=np.maximum(A[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,A.shape[1]); Mn=np.minimum(A[:,None,:],A[None,:,:]).reshape(-1,A.shape[1])
    return set(map(tuple,J.tolist()))<=Xs and set(map(tuple,Mn.tolist()))<=Xs
print('|Λ9| =',len(L9),'; E(Λ9) = 0 (join/meet of all pairs in Λ9):',E0(L9),'; projection of Λ9 onto its first 8 coordinates == Λ8:',set(c[:8] for c in L9)==S8, '(L769–770)')
for name,X,d in (('Λ8',L8,8),('Λ9',L9,9)):
    s=[sum(c) for c in X]; b=min(s)
    print('%s: F(−1) with rank = Σx_i: %d ; with graded rank Σx_i − %d: %d  (L771 "F(−1) = 2 unchanged")'%(name,sum((-1)**v for v in s),b,sum((-1)**(v-b) for v in s)))
# join-irreducibles of Λ8 (exactly one lower cover), covers among them, Birkhoff down-sets
def leq(a,b): return all(x<=y for x,y in zip(a,b))
def lower_covers(c):
    below=[d for d in L8 if d!=c and leq(d,c)]
    return [d for d in below if not any(e!=d and e!=c and leq(d,e) and leq(e,c) for e in below)]
J=[c for c in L8 if len(lower_covers(c))==1]
print('|J(Λ8)| =',len(J),'(L852 "|J(Λ)| = 17"; L8517 "|J(Λ)| = 17 = height")')
Jc=[(a,b) for a in J for b in J if a!=b and leq(a,b) and not any(e!=a and e!=b and leq(a,e) and leq(e,b) for e in J)]
print('covering relations within J(Λ8):',len(Jc),'(L853 "twenty covering relations"; L854–855 "twenty implications")')
idx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(J)}; up={i:[idx[b] for (a,b) in Jc if a==J[i]] for i in range(len(J))}
downsets=0
for mask in range(1<<len(J)):
    ok=True
    for i in range(len(J)):
        if mask>>i&1:
            for (a,b) in Jc:
                if b==J[i] and not (mask>>idx[a]&1): ok=False; break
            if not ok: break
    downsets+=ok
print('down-sets of J(Λ8) (Birkhoff):',downsets,'of 2^%d = %d words (L853 "976"; L855 "131,072 words to 976")'%(len(J),1<<len(J)))
A=np.array(L8); sizes=[len(set(A[:,i])) for i in range(8)]
print('alphabet Σ(|A_i| − 1) =',sum(s-1 for s in sizes),'from |A_i| =',sizes,'(L853 "17")')
B=np.array(L13); box=int(np.prod([B[:,i].max()-B[:,i].min()+1 for i in range(13)]))
print('ambient box of Λ13 = ∏ ranges =',box,'(L856, L993 "47,775,744"); Λ8 box =',int(np.prod([A[:,i].max()-A[:,i].min()+1 for i in range(8)])))

No §2.21 or §2.22 heading exists (`^#+ *2\.2[12]`: 0). MEASURED. READING: two protocols named by the book are not in the chapter; the census (C1, 8 unresolved) did not report these four pointers.

**2-02 · L598 (§2.6) against §23.11.** PRINTED: "Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §23.11 gives a worked case of each." SOURCE: §23.11 L6519 "The refusal pattern carries four verdicts, not one" — its four are refusal patterns (none/infinite V; none/finite; one; regularly spaced; dense and irregular) and L6519–6570 contain none of the four causes' names. That was true at registers 630–631 and was overtaken by the parent-term wall (register 1578) and the J-resolved rows of T8-J (registers 1699–1700); the table drifted from…"; L10277 also prints "across all 153 channels". **2-04 · L701 (§2.15.2) against its own table L683–699.** PRINTED: "Two lower bounds, two upper, two negatives, five structural, one methodological" (= 12) over "Ten consecutive failures". The kind column of the ten rows reads upper, lower, negative, structural, upper, method, negative, lower, structural, structural — 2 / 2 / 2 / 3 / 1 = 10. MEASURED (page).  The three were obtained separately and their identity had to be computed, so unlike the Rydberg case
 it is not a tautology. **One definition, three dimensions, each a perspective of it** — which is
 what P9 says. Register 429.

 **Two are relations** — P7 and P17 — and each carried an expression that could not be evaluated,
 which is why. An expression is a mechanism's form and a relation is not a mechanism. Both keep their
 content and lose their expressions, exactly as §1 already says is better than manufacturing one.

 **And four mechanisms were stated without something they need.**

 **P2 needs its hypothesis, and the hypothesis has a name.** ⅅ ≥ dim q − rank ∂Φ/∂p ≥ dim q − dim p,
 so **ⅅ ≥ 1 exactly when dim q > dim p** — when the index derives strictly more quantities than it
 assigns parameters. That is **surplus**, which §11.1.1 measures at 7.07 bits per cell and Chapter 16
 states in prose as *it found it because it carried more than it needed*. For Λ the bound is tight:
 dim p = 4, dim q = 6, rank 4, ⅅ = 2. **Without surplus there is no check**, which is Edlén's
 footnote 78.

 **P7's well-founded measure, which this book demanded and never supplied, is already computed in
 Appendix E.** The measure is not the count of open items — §1 shows why — but the **multiset of
 their `blocks` values** under the ordering *nothing < a novelty assessment < one stated claim < a
 result the book relies on*. That coordinate is ordered and bounded below, so it is well-founded, and
 the multiset extension of a well-founded order is well-founded. Checked against §29.2.1's own
 movement, where six items' stake fell to nothing: the count went 13 → 10 and the multiset decreased
 in the Dershowitz–Manna sense. **That is precisely what *the set grew and the scope descended*
 means.**

 **P17's 1/N is derivable and the constant was dropped.** §10.3 decides whether a box lies inside Λ
 in **seven comparisons**, against one membership test per cell for enumeration. So following the
 bounds costs **c/N with c the number of constraints**, c = 7 here — 7/976 on Λ, 7/199,130 on Λ₁₃.
 **And N is nowhere defined**: neither §18.4 nor Chapter 12 introduces it, so the symbol is
 ungrounded in the sense §16.6's ⅅ_gro names. The corrected form carries no N: *following the bounds
 costs one comparison per constraint where searching the volume costs one per cell.*

 **P22 claimed what §16.8.2 refutes.** *No lie can exist within it* is false: rebuilt around a
 fabrication the index closes, has E = 0, is a fixed point of ℛ and satisfies every law here.
 Restated: **in a complete index every rule is content rather than inference, so a false cell is
 contradicted in the open by a stated rule where an inferred rule would have absorbed it. A forger's
 remaining move is to alter a rule, and an altered rule is equally visible. A complete index
 therefore converts deception into disagreement — error survives, concealment does not.** The index
 cannot be lied **to**; it can be **replaced**, and replacement is an act performed on it rather than
 a question put to it. Registers 417–420.

 Procedural — seven

| | principle |
|---|---|
| **P4** | always audit results |
| **P5** | always compute the result before assuming the result |
| **P6** | when a question is confusing, reframe the question |
| **P11** | close all gaps before continuing |
| **P14** | a structural problem suggests a structural solution |
| **P15** | for fetching: use the index to navigate; data can be retrieved in pieces |
| **P16** | treat bounds, constraints and limits as coordinate values |

 **These have no expressions, and saying so is better than manufacturing one.** They govern how an agent uses an index, not what an index is. P15 is the exception in one respect: it has a *measure* — retrieval redundancy ρ, Chapter 19 — without being reducible to it.

 The reflexive principle

        principle                                                                                              expression
  P1    if the index is complete, a work that comprehends it completely is itself an index, and is itself      Chapter 32
  8     self-referencing and self-defending
  P1    an index is complete only when there are no more questions left to answer about its                    COMPLETE(X)
  9     contents                                                                                               ⟺ Q(X) = ∅
  P2    the language in which a question is posed bounds whether it can close, and at what                     —
  0     cost
  P2    any definition contained within the lattice, and thus its equations, must be TRUE in                   —
  1     every mathematical language and in their combinations
  P2    because everything is defined in a complete index, the entirety of the index is                        —
  2     visible, and no lie can exist within it

 P19, and why it is neither P7 nor P13
 Three principles govern questions, and they are one principle in three moods. P19 was the
 missing one.

| | says | mood |
|---|---|---|
| **P7** | ∃N : Ω_N = ∅ | questions **can** close — possibility |
| **P13** | COHERENT ⟺ Ω = ∅ | coherence **may not** be claimed otherwise — prohibition |
| **P19** | COMPLETE ⟺ Q = ∅ | what their emptiness **buys** — definition |

 **And P19 is strictly stronger than closure.**

      E(X) = 0 says no cell the structure admits is absent. Q(X) = ∅ says no question the
      contents admit is unanswered.

 **Λ has had E = 0 since Chapter 7 and has never had Q = ∅.** Whether *V* depends on the order of the bracket, what the Aitken bias generalises to, whether a higher-order bracket exists — **each was admitted by contents already present, and none was asked until late.**

      Closure is about what an index holds. Completeness is about what it has been asked.

 **And the condition is reachable, for the reason P7's is.** P7 was corrected once: closure requires a well-founded measure rather than a shrinking count. **Q has grown at nearly every step of this work while its scope has fallen** — from *is V novel?* to *is there an optimal order?* **The set grew and the scope descended**, and that descent is what makes P19 a criterion rather than an impossibility.

 **Q(X) = ∅ is reached not when nobody asks, but when every question the contents admit has an answer in the contents.**

 P20 — the language bounds the question
 Three closure mechanisms are used in this book, each in a different language, each with a
 different guarantee.

| language | mechanism | closure | cost |

568	## 2. The protocols
   569	### 2.1 Channel construction
   570	    A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.
   571	
   572	 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.
   573	
   574	### 2.2 Admissibility
   575	    r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5
   576	
   577	 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.
   578	
   579	### 2.3 Cost resolvability
   580	    ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}
   581	
   582	 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.
   583	
   584	### 2.4 Dilution
   585	    cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
   586	    configuration
   587	
   588	 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.
   589	
   590	### 2.5 Census before search
   591	    Compute which species could work before looking for data.
   592	
   593	 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**
   594	
   595	### 2.6 Declines are recorded
   596	    A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.
   597	
   598	 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §23.11 gives a worked case of each.
   599	
   600	### 2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible
   601	
   602	    Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
   603	    never certifies ρ = 0.
   604	
   605	 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.
   606	
   607	### 2.8 Two independent routes
   608	    For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
   609	    first.
   610	
   611	 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 16, and it is realised
   612	 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §16.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
   613	 with no shared step.
   614	
   615	 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.
   616	
   617	### 2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
   618	    No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.
   619	
   620	 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.
   621	
   622	### 2.10 Retrieval
   623	    Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
   624	    cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
   625	    along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
   626	    targets are drawn from grows.
   627	
   628	 Chapter 19. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.
   629	
   630	 The second clause was added late. §30.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
   631	 §30.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §31.1, §31.2 and §31.3 — each made once, against
   632	 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.
   633	
   634	    Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
   635	    is a defect the moment it is taken.
   636	
   637	### 2.11 Provenance
   638	    Every number traces to a compilation, table and page, or to a database entry with its
   639	    stated uncertainty.
   640	
   641	 Appendix B carries this at channel level for all 153 channels.
   642	
   643	### 2.12 Withdrawal
   644	    Every retracted claim is logged with what replaced it.
   645	
   646	 Chapter 28. one thousand six hundred and thirty-five entries. The register is the evidence for Chapter 16, not
   647	 an apology for it.
   648	
   649	### 2.13 Commit before you look
   650	    A prediction is written down before the measurement is requested. A method is chosen
   651	    before its answer is visible.
   652	
   653	 **This is the process index of §28.8 enforced by hand:** the constraint **visible ≤ committed**, of §16.4 form, closed, E = 0.
   654	
   655	 **It is the only protocol here adopted in response to an error that no computation could have caught** — because every computation was correct and what failed was the independence of a choice. **The deduction of §25.6 was committed under it.**
   656	
   657	### 2.14 Compute, then write
   658	    The result is computed before the sentence describing it is written.
   659	
   660	 **This is the protocol most often violated in the production of this book.** The dominant failure recorded in Chapter 28 is prose asserting a conclusion while the output contradicting it stands on the same screen. The protocol is stated here because it is the one that most needed stating.
   661	
   662	### 2.15 Apply P8 to every failure
   663	    Every failed attempt is a true answer, and by P8 a true answer is a bound. Record what
   664	    each failure excludes, and collect the exclusions.
   665	
   666	 P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
   667	 where the target is not. The protocol is to treat it that way rather than discard it.
   668	
   669	### 2.15.1 The procedure
   670	 On each failure, write down three things:
   671	
   672	  what was attempted                     the claim or construction
   673	  what it excludes                       the region of the answer space now ruled out
   674	  which kind                             upper bound · lower bound · negative · structural
   675	
   676	 Then read the collection. Lower bounds say the answer contains something; upper bounds say it is
   677	 contained in something; negatives remove whole methods; structural failures name an object that was
   678	 the wrong one. When the lower and upper bounds meet, the answer is between them.
   679	
   680	### 2.15.2 Worked, on §30.3
   681	 Ten consecutive failures on one question, each read as a bound:
   682	
   683	  the failure                                              the bound                                               kind
   684	  Γ-free ≠ reorderable                                     reorderable ⊊ totally balanced                          upper
   685	  chain sufficient, not necessary                          chain ⊊ reorderable                                     lower
   686	  depth-2 and depth-3 descent stall, worsening with        no constant-depth local procedure decides it            negati
   687	  size                                                                                                             ve
   688	  linear extensions of the inclusion order incomplete      the inclusion order is not the join-irreducible poset   struct
   689	                                                                                                                   ural
   690	  the slice-chain condition fails at d = 3                 the d = 2 condition does not lift                       upper
   691	  the 3-SAT encoding was refuted                           a reduction must control which pairs arise              metho
   692	                                                                                                                   d
   693	  descent traps at E = 1, 2                                the transposition landscape is not convex               negati
   694	                                                                                                                   ve
   695	  occupancy sort succeeds 53%                              tie-breaking among equal occupancy is not free          lower
   696	  "row chain or column chain" holds at 68%                 neither axis alone decides it; the condition is         struct
   697	                                                           two-sided                                               ural
   698	  the chain criterion characterises the downset            ℛ-closure and downset-closure differ by the direction   struct
   699	  operator, not ℛ                                          of one axis                                             ural
   700	
   701	 Two lower bounds, two upper, two negatives, five structural, one methodological. Between
   702	 them: reorderable ⊋ chain and ⊊ totally balanced, and the gap contains at least the diagonals —
   703	 which is what produced the characterisation:
   704	
   705	    X is ℛ-closed iff X = {(r,c) : c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c)}, with M\, N\ the running maxima of its own
   706	    row and column maxima.
   707	
   708	 Ten failures produced one exact statement. None of them was wasted, and none of them would have
   709	 been kept without the protocol.
   710	
   711	 And the last two are the ones that located it. The two-sided bound said neither axis decides alone;
   712	 the operator bound said the borrowed condition belonged to a different closure. Together they force
   713	 the form c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c), which no single-axis condition can express and which the two-cell
   714	 diagonal {(0,0), (1,1)} realises minimally.
   715	
   716	### 2.15.3 Why it belongs here rather than among the principles
   717	 It says nothing about what an index is. It is a way of working, and it is the reason Chapter 28 is the
   718	 longest chapter in this book rather than the most embarrassing.
   719	
   720	    A register of withdrawals is a list of bounds. Read it that way and it stops being a
   721	    confession.
   722	
   723	### 2.16 The grid — the book's method, stated
   724	 Every open question is a set of requirements, and requirements form an index. Lay them as a
   725	 grid, mark what is occupied, and read the empty cells rather than hunting for them.
   726	
   727	    The first empty cell in a column is the whole obstacle. Everything below it is downstream.
   728	
   729	### 2.16.1 Why this is the method and not a technique
   730	 It is Chapter 6 applied to the book's own ignorance. A periodic table with 36 unfilled cells does not
   731	 need a chemist to guess which are missing — the layout shows them. An open question with eight
   732	 unfilled requirements does not need twenty-two attempts — the grid shows that four of them are one.
   733	
   734	 Worked on §30.3: eight empty cells, four rows deep, at d ≥ 3.
   735	
   736	  requirement                     d=2                                d≥3
   737	  characterisation                proved                             ·
   738	  decision procedure              linear                             ·
   739	  YES certificate                 an order                           an order
   740	  NO certificate                  Tucker — unbounded                 unbounded
   741	  obstruction family              Tucker 1972                        unbounded, route closed
   742	  construction rules              six preserving                     six preserving
   743	  hardness                        P, the CSP is binary               ·
   744	  the data structure              PQ-tree                            ·
   745	
   746	    Three rows are full at every d, and they are the three that needed no d-specific work —
   747	    the certificate is the order itself, the obstruction family is Tucker's, the construction rules were
   748	    established once. Every empty cell is downstream of one missing object: the d ≥ 3 analogue
   749	    of a PQ-tree.
   750	
   751	 Twenty-two formulations were attempts on four cells that depend on one. The grid says so in
   752	 a table; hunting concealed it for a day.
   753	
   754	### 2.16.2 And it classifies the whole of Q
   755	
   756	  item                             first empty cell                       the obstacle
   757	  Sc VI 6s                         the level is measured                  an instrument
   758	  Paschen & Götze                  the scan is text-searchable            a digitisation artefact

## 2. The protocols
### 2.1 Channel construction
    A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.

 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.

### 2.2 Admissibility
    r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5

 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.

### 2.3 Cost resolvability
    ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}

 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.

### 2.4 Dilution
    cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
    configuration

 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.

### 2.5 Census before search
    Compute which species could work before looking for data.

 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**

### 2.6 Declines are recorded
    A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.

 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §23.11 gives a worked case of each.

### 2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible

    Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
    never certifies ρ = 0.

 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.

### 2.8 Two independent routes
    For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
    first.

 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 16, and it is realised
 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §16.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
 with no shared step.

 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.

### 2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
    No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.

 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.

### 2.10 Retrieval
    Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
    cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
    along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
    targets are drawn from grows.

 Chapter 19. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.

 The second clause was added late. §30.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
 §30.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §31.1, §31.2 and §31.3 — each made once, against
 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.

    Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
    is a defect the moment it is taken.

### 2.11 Provenance
    Every number traces to a compilation, table and page, or to a database entry with its
    stated uncertainty.

 Appendix B carries this at channel level for all 153 channels.

### 2.12 Withdrawal
    Every retracted claim is logged with what replaced it.

 Chapter 28. one thousand six hundred and thirty-five entries. The register is the evidence for Chapter 16, not
 an apology for it.

### 2.13 Commit before you look
    A prediction is written down before the measurement is requested. A method is chosen
    before its answer is visible.

 **This is the process index of §28.8 enforced by hand:** the constraint **visible ≤ committed**, of §16.4 form, closed, E = 0.

 **It is the only protocol here adopted in response to an error that no computation could have caught** — because every computation was correct and what failed was the independence of a choice. **The deduction of §25.6 was committed under it.**

### 2.14 Compute, then write
    The result is computed before the sentence describing it is written.

 **This is the protocol most often violated in the production of this book.** The dominant failure recorded in Chapter 28 is prose asserting a conclusion while the output contradicting it stands on the same screen. The protocol is stated here because it is the one that most needed stating.

### 2.15 Apply P8 to every failure
    Every failed attempt is a true answer, and by P8 a true answer is a bound. Record what
    each failure excludes, and collect the exclusions.

 P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
 where the target is not. The protocol is to treat it that way rather than discard it.

### 2.15.1 The procedure
 On each failure, write down three things:

  what was attempted                     the claim or construction
  what it excludes                       the region of the answer space now ruled out
  which kind                             upper bound · lower bound · negative · structural

 Then read the collection. Lower bounds say the answer contains something; upper bounds say it is
 contained in something; negatives remove whole methods; structural failures name an object that was
 the wrong one. When the lower and upper bounds meet, the answer is between them.

### 2.15.2 Worked, on §30.3
 Ten consecutive failures on one question, each read as a bound:

  the failure                                              the bound                                               kind
  Γ-free ≠ reorderable                                     reorderable ⊊ totally balanced                          upper
  chain sufficient, not necessary                          chain ⊊ reorderable                                     lower
  depth-2 and depth-3 descent stall, worsening with        no constant-depth local procedure decides it            negati
  size                                                                                                             ve
  linear extensions of the inclusion order incomplete      the inclusion order is not the join-irreducible poset   struct
                                                                                                                   ural
  the slice-chain condition fails at d = 3                 the d = 2 condition does not lift                       upper
  the 3-SAT encoding was refuted                           a reduction must control which pairs arise              metho
                                                                                                                   d
  descent traps at E = 1, 2                                the transposition landscape is not convex               negati
                                                                                                                   ve
  occupancy sort succeeds 53%                              tie-breaking among equal occupancy is not free          lower
  "row chain or column chain" holds at 68%                 neither axis alone decides it; the condition is         struct
                                                           two-sided                                               ural
  the chain criterion characterises the downset            ℛ-closure and downset-closure differ by the direction   struct
  operator, not ℛ                                          of one axis                                             ural

 Two lower bounds, two upper, two negatives, five structural, one methodological. Between
 them: reorderable ⊋ chain and ⊊ totally balanced, and the gap contains at least the diagonals —
 which is what produced the characterisation:

    X is ℛ-closed iff X = {(r,c) : c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c)}, with M\, N\ the running maxima of its own
    row and column maxima.

 Ten failures produced one exact statement. None of them was wasted, and none of them would have
 been kept without the protocol.

 And the last two are the ones that located it. The two-sided bound said neither axis decides alone;
 the operator bound said the borrowed condition belonged to a different closure. Together they force
 the form c ≤ M\(r) and r ≤ N\(c), which no single-axis condition can express and which the two-cell
 diagonal {(0,0), (1,1)} realises minimally.

### 2.15.3 Why it belongs here rather than among the principles
 It says nothing about what an index is. It is a way of working, and it is the reason Chapter 28 is the
 longest chapter in this book rather than the most embarrassing.

    A register of withdrawals is a list of bounds. Read it that way and it stops being a
    confession.

### 2.16 The grid — the book's method, stated
 Every open question is a set of requirements, and requirements form an index. Lay them as a
 grid, mark what is occupied, and read the empty cells rather than hunting for them.

    The first empty cell in a column is the whole obstacle. Everything below it is downstream.

### 2.16.1 Why this is the method and not a technique
 It is Chapter 6 applied to the book's own ignorance. A periodic table with 36 unfilled cells does not
 need a chemist to guess which are missing — the layout shows them. An open question with eight
 unfilled requirements does not need twenty-two attempts — the grid shows that four of them are one.

 Worked on §30.3: eight empty cells, four rows deep, at d ≥ 3.

  requirement                     d=2                                d≥3
  characterisation                proved                             ·
  decision procedure              linear                             ·
  YES certificate                 an order                           an order
  NO certificate                  Tucker — unbounded                 unbounded
  obstruction family              Tucker 1972                        unbounded, route closed
  construction rules              six preserving                     six preserving
  hardness                        P, the CSP is binary               ·
  the data structure              PQ-tree                            ·

    Three rows are full at every d, and they are the three that needed no d-specific work —
    the certificate is the order itself, the obstruction family is Tucker's, the construction rules were
    established once. Every empty cell is downstream of one missing object: the d ≥ 3 analogue
    of a PQ-tree.

 Twenty-two formulations were attempts on four cells that depend on one. The grid says so in
 a table; hunting concealed it for a day.

### 2.16.2 And it classifies the whole of Q

  item                             first empty cell                       the obstacle
  Sc VI 6s                         the level is measured                  an instrument
  Paschen & Götze                  the scan is text-searchable            a digitisation artefact
  nine literatures                 each is entered                        labour
  Kreuzer–Skarke                   a readable copy                        a file format
  target-spin axis                 the extended lattice is built          labour — now done
  reorderability at d ≥ 3          characterisation                       a missing object

 Five of six were blocked by something outside the index. One is blocked by something that
 does not exist. §32.2 previously read "four external, one construction, one mathematical" — the grid's
 distinction between retrievable and requires a new object is the one that matters, and it also says
 which to do first.

 The target-spin axis was taken on that basis and it closed. Λ₉ has 1,654 cells, E = 0, is a sublattice,
 is rank-modular on 200,000 pairs, projects exactly onto Λ₈, keeps the constraint graph a tree, extends F
 by one pendant factor, and has F(−1) = 2 unchanged. One unit of labour, six properties confirmed,
 \|Q\| from six to five.

### 2.16.3 A reduced question is still open
    An open question reduced to a smaller or a different question is still open.

 A reduction feels like progress and reads like an answer. §30.3 supplies five in one session, each
 announced as a closure:

  the reduction                                                             what was still open
  reorderability ⟹ C1P + monotone endpoints                                 the endpoint search
  the search ⟹ a PQ-tree frontier question                                  a correct PQ-tree
  the frontier question ⟹ a bottom-up traversal                             the traversal's state
  the traversal ⟹ a row→node anchoring map                                  rows anchoring as runs
  the whole problem ⟹ a CSP on axis orders                                  the ternary constraints

 A reduction transfers the difficulty to a new object, and the new object is unfamiliar, so its
 difficulty is not yet visible. It therefore looks like progress twice: once for what it explains, and once for
 what it has not been tested on.

State the reduction and the residue in the same sentence. Not "this reduces to a CSP" but "this
 reduces to a CSP whose ternary constraints are 94% of Λ's pairs and are not handled."

### 2.17 Triangulation — three results locate a fourth
    For every three results or bounds that measure the same object, triangulate: they
    identify a related data point that none of them states.

 Three measurements of one thing are not three facts. They are a position.

### 2.17.1 Worked, from §30.3

  the three                              what they                  the fourth, located
                                         measured
  valid orders disconnected ·            connectivity failure in    the disconnection is in the object, not the space —
  E-landscape traps · cell-growth        three different spaces     so no local method in any space can be complete
  peaks
  step 1 at d = 2 · step 2 at d = 3 ·    growth step, three         step = 2^(d−2), then proved by subcube removal
  step 4 at d = 4                        dimensions
  arity 2 bijunctive · arity 3           the constraint             the boundary is arity 3 and it is exact — the
  bijunctive · arity 4 contains          language                   procedure and the hardness proof are one law read at two
  1-in-3-SAT                                                        arities
  three reductions, all                  the encoding               the map X → C(X) is global, non-separable and
  over-constraining                                                 non-monotone — it admits no local editing

 Each fourth point was invisible in any single measurement and forced by the three together.
 The step law is the clearest: 1, 2, 4 fixed the ¾ ratio, and the ratio gave the subcube construction, which
 proved it.

### 2.17.2 And it is a check as well as a method
 Triangulation fails loudly. If three measurements of one object do not locate a consistent fourth, one of
 them is wrong — and that is how three corrections were caught in a single session:

 A map that is global, non-separable and non-monotone should have a SMALL image.
 Measured: 39% at d = 3 and 49.5% at d = 4, rising. The three coordinates were right and the
 inference from them was not — they locate an obstruction to EDITING the map, not to its range.

    Three consistent measurements give a fourth result. Three measurements that give no
    consistent fourth give a correction instead. Both outcomes are useful and the protocol does not
    distinguish them in advance.

### 2.17.3 Why it belongs with the protocols
 It is P8 with a count attached. Every failure is a bound; three bounds on one object are a
 coordinate. §2.15 says to record failures as bounds; this says what to do once three of them are in
 hand.

 And it composes with §2.16. The grid shows which cells are empty; triangulation fills one from three
 of its neighbours.


### 2.18 What is computable, and what is decided
 §3.8 ends by saying a coordinate system answers to two masters and only one of them is
 computable. The word is doing real work and the book has not defined it. It defines it with its own
 operator.

    **A quantity is COMPUTABLE in this book when it is recoverable by ℛ from what the book
    prints** — when two readers running the stated procedure on the printed text return the same
    value, and neither has to decide anything to get there.

 That is not a claim about difficulty. E(Λ) = 0 over 475,800 pairs is computable and took minutes;
 whether A.5's language is order or analysis is not computable and took one sentence.

 **Nineteen quantities in the work of these sessions are computable.** E(Λ) = 0; |J(Λ)| = 17 with its
 twenty covering relations; the Birkhoff down-set count of 976; the alphabet's size Σ(|Aᵢ| − 1) = 17;
 the seventeen-bit encoding with join as OR and meet as AND; the 7.07 bits of surplus; the twenty
 implications cutting 131,072 words to 976; every tower cell count and every density; closure through
 the f shell at 499,246 cells and exhaustively to 47,775,744 ambient ones; the E1 puncture at four
 meets all producing (0,0); the triangle at four caps; lemma 4 over 2,354 interval sets; E(audits) at
 11, 0 and 19; dim(audit hierarchy) = 2; E(G), recomputed at build; E(Q); the tripwire's 150 of 216; the fifty-four
 of one hundred and two. **Each is a function of the printed object and of nothing else.**

 **Ten are decisions, and they are of three kinds.**

 *Frames.* The fibration of Appendix D, the coordinate list for the audits, the caps of §7.4. E is
 computable **given** them and none of them is computed — register 275 is the general statement, that
 a zero is worth the size of the box it was computed in, and the box is chosen.

 *Readings.* Applying a stated criterion to a case it does not settle: whether A.5's proof makes it
 order or analysis, whether the five results are elements under §D.5.3, whether *law* means
 holds-of-every-index or holds-and-forbids. The criterion is printed; the application is a judgement,
 and §D.5.4 marks the one place this work made one and says so.

 *Claims about the outside.* Precedent, novelty, whether a measurement exists. §29.1 proves the first
 of these permanently undecidable in one direction, which is the strongest statement of this kind the
 book contains.

 **And the distinction has a use, not merely a name.** Every computable quantity in this book can be
 checked by a reader with the printed text and no access to its author. Every decision must be
 *stated* rather than checked, and the register is what stating them costs. **The seven prime audits
 of §3.1–7 test computable claims; nothing tests a decision**, which is why the seventeenth
 through twentieth entries of the register are corrections of computation and the twentieth through
 fortieth are reversals of judgement. The book cannot make its decisions checkable. It can make them
 visible, and that is the whole of what the register is for. Register 277.

### 2.18.1 The lattice applied to what it cannot compute
 §2.18 separates nineteen computed quantities from ten decisions and stops there, on the ground
 that nothing tests a decision. **The shape still applies to them, and it says two things.**

 **First: index the decisions and E finds one that has not been made.** Coordinates *scope*, *how it
 is stated* and *reversibility*, fibred by kind — frame, reading, outside claim. Ten decisions,
 E = 1 fibred and 5 unfibred, with a single cell admitted and absent in the *reading* fibre:

    a reading, scoped to one appendix, stated, freely reversible.

 That cell has an occupant the book declined to seat. Register 270 records that Appendices B and F — then lettered C and G —
 are cited from the body only as wholes and never at section level, calls it a navigability defect,
 and leaves the choice open. **It is a reading, it is confined to two appendices, it is stated, and it
 costs nothing to reverse.** E over the decisions located a deferred decision exactly as E over Q
 located item H — which is the first evidence that the operator has any purchase outside the
 computable.

 **Second, and this is the finding: the decisions form a DAG, and two of them have two parents.**
 The order is acyclic, so the decisions can be made in some sequence and none presupposes itself. Six
 of the ten depend on nothing. But two do not have a single parent:

    the fibration of Appendix D — settled only with the caps of §7.4 **and** what counts as an
    element both in view

    not promoting the six theorems — settled only with the meaning of *law* **and** the audit
    coordinate list both in view

 **This is §12.11's dichotomy, arriving in the one place the book had assumed it did not reach.** A
 single-parent constraint propagates down a tree and is carried exactly; a two-parent constraint
 breaks the tree and admits only an envelope. The tight K has two parents and costs the cylinder
 2,475 cells. A two-parent *decision* is the same shape: **no earlier choice determines it, and it
 cannot be delegated to one predecessor or deferred until one is settled.** It must be made with both
 in view or not at all.

 **And with the fourth node of §18.4.1 the count goes to three.** In a triangle every node has degree
 two, so a decision has at most two parents; in K₄ every node has degree three. **Three-parent
 decisions exist and each resisted for the same reason** — none can be delegated to one predecessor
 or deferred until one is settled:

  the decision                        its three parents
  is Λ the clean control?             the object (976 cells, E = 0) · the law (what E = 0 certifies) ·
                                      reference (seven of thirteen letters conflated)
  is the closure rule correct?        the object (Λ closes) · the law (the admissibility criterion) ·
                                      reference (what *monotone* names in the constraint literature)
  is E(audits) meaningful?            the procedure (the set) · the law (the coordinate list, a frame) ·
                                      reference (whether *audit* means one thing across it)

 **Two instances was not a law and three is not much better**, which §18.4.1 says of its own
 prediction and which this section repeats of the extension. What is worth recording is that the
 three were not gathered for the test: each arrived as a difficulty before the shape was drawn.
 Register 407.

 The book has two such decisions and it stumbled on both. Registers 219 to 222 hold three successive
 positions on the element count, which is the fibration decision made once with the caps in view and
 once with the element criterion in view and never with both. Register 232 declines the promotion and
 says the reason is a trade between two things at once. **Two instances is not a law**, and the
 correspondence is offered as what it is — a shape that fits twice, in a set of ten, where the
 prediction it makes is that any third two-parent decision will be hard in the same way. Register 278.

### 2.19 What a safe repair requires
 §3.8 recorded a defect and declined to repair it on the ground that the repair was riskier
 than the defect. That judgement was made without a standard, and this states one.

    A repair is **safe** when five conditions hold. **(i)** Its invariant is written down before
    the edit — what must be true afterwards that was true before. **(ii)** The invariant is
    computable in the sense of §2.18, so it can be checked rather than asserted. **(iii)** The
    edit is a *permutation or an insertion*, never a rewrite: existing text is moved, not retyped,
    so no character can change unnoticed. **(iv)** It is reversible — a copy is taken first and
    restored if the check fails. **(v)** It is checked afterwards on the source **and** the
    artefact, because §3's FIDELITY exists for the gap between them.

 **And a sixth that governs which repair to attempt: prefer the smallest edit that removes the
 defect.** A defect visible in a hundred places is not therefore a hundred-place repair. Applying
 that here changed what the repair was.

### 2.19.1 The register, examined before repairing it
 The recorded defect was direction: entries 165 to 204 ascending, 205 onward descending. Measuring
 the register against its own headings found something larger and cheaper to fix. Each subsection of
 §28.7 states a count in its title — *Eight more*, *Twelve more*, *Fifteen more*, *Forty more* — and
 **§28.7.6 was titled "Three from the tower session" and contained eighty-six entries, 199 to 284**,
 every entry written since that session having been prepended into it. It is now four — the tower's
 three, which repairs their numbering — and §28.7.7 the eighty-seven written
 afterwards.

 **That is the defect worth repairing**, and it is one heading rather than a hundred and twenty
 entries. The direction is a presentation choice made twice; the heading is a false statement of
 count, which audit 15 ENUMERATION exists to catch and which it missed because it was pointed at
 tables and lists rather than at section titles. Register 286.

### 2.20 The prime directive — nothing runs unbounded
 Every action, computation, tabulation, build and verification is executed in a **Zeno structure**: the
 work is divided until each piece fits inside a declared budget, each piece writes its result before
 the next begins, and a rerun costs only what has not already succeeded.

 **One exception, and it is the only one.** **Fetched literature is exempt.** A computation may be
 halved and rerun on half; an external source cannot, because halving what was read changes what was
 read. A source consulted at half length is a different source, and the register would carry a claim
 about a document nobody has seen. So a fetch runs to completion or is not made, and the budget is
 declared before it rather than enforced during it. Register 432.

    **No operation runs unbounded.** A step declares a budget; work that exceeds it is halved and
    retried; a step that has succeeded is never recomputed.

 **Three guarantees, and they are the reason for the rule.** Nothing is lost to a timeout, because the
 last completed step is on disk before the next starts. A rerun costs only the remainder. And a step
 that overruns **reports its overrun** rather than dying silently — which is the part that matters
 most, since a computation quietly growing toward a limit is invisible until the run it kills.

 **Why this book needs it.** Audit 1 tests 475,800 pairs; the exhaustive closure of §12.11 swept
 47,775,744 ambient cells; the f-shell rebuild of §32.1.2 carried 499,246. Each of those was run whole
 and none had a fallback. The harness is *zeno.py*, the state is *.zeno/*, and §2.20's requirement
 that the audits run on every output now runs under it: the twenty write their state, and an
 interrupted pass resumes rather than restarting.

 **What it does not do.** It does not make a slow computation fast, and it does not decide anything —
 a step that fails is retained with its error for retry, not silently skipped. The budget is a
 declaration about what is expected, so an overrun is a finding about the computation and belongs in
 the register like any other. Register 343.
